title: New Scientist Story Ideas — August 2026

studies.title: Relaxation exercises may make some talk therapies work less well, huge patient-level analysis finds
studies.ns_score_reason: individual participant data from more than 10,000 people, and the headline result is that two staples of therapy look actively unhelpful.
studies.the_study: Researchers pooled individual participant data from 30 randomized trials (10,612 adults; 72% women, mean age 36.7) of psychosocial interventions for depression and anxiety delivered by non-specialists, then dismantled each therapy into its constituent ingredients and ran a Bayesian component network meta-analysis. Strengthening social support was by far the most beneficial component (incremental mean difference −9.48), followed by behavioral activation and problem management. Relaxation training was associated with a worse outcome (+7.97), and cognitive reframing was also on the detrimental side (+5.17). Component effects varied by baseline severity and demographics, and the team built a web app that generates personalized estimates.
studies.why_it_matters: If replicated, this challenges the assumption that adding more therapeutic ingredients makes a package better — and suggests the "active drug" in scalable global mental health programs is social connection, not the relaxation and thought-challenging exercises many people associate with therapy.
studies.pitch_angle: "The bit of therapy that might be holding you back." Open with someone doing progressive muscle relaxation homework from a self-help app, then reveal that in the largest component-level analysis to date, relaxation was the one ingredient linked to worse symptom outcomes. Call Davide Papola (University of Verona/Harvard Medical School) and co-author Pim Cuijpers; ask a UK CBT trialist for pushback, since cognitive reframing is a core CBT component and the trials here were task-shared, often in humanitarian settings.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a global health or policy outlet on the "dismantling" movement in psychotherapy research — the push to treat therapies like drug formularies with identifiable active components and dosages, and what a WHO-funded personalization web app means for delivering mental health care in countries with almost no psychiatrists.
studies.caveats: Components are inferred from a purpose-built taxonomy rather than randomized head-to-head, so "detrimental" components may be confounded by which trials used them; ethnicity data unavailable; trials were largely in low-resource and humanitarian settings, so generalization to specialist Western care is uncertain; funded by the European Commission; one author declares pharmaceutical and app-related interests.

studies.title: Psychological first aid after trauma performs worse than doing nothing in a randomized trial
studies.ns_score_reason: a randomized test of one of the world's most widely promoted post-disaster interventions, with a genuinely uncomfortable result; limited by the analogue stress paradigm.
studies.the_study: Eighty-four participants watched a validated distressing video, then were randomized to group Psychological First Aid (n=47) or natural recovery (n=37), with 74 followed up two weeks later. The control group showed a greater reduction in stress immediately after the intervention (medium effect size), and by two weeks the groups were indistinguishable overall — except that participants who had been most distressed at the outset reported significantly more trauma symptoms at follow-up if they had received PFA.
studies.why_it_matters: PFA has been rolled out globally as the safe, evidence-neutral replacement for critical incident stress debriefing; this trial suggests it may share debriefing's central flaw of interfering with natural recovery in exactly the people it targets.
studies.pitch_angle: "The trauma intervention we replaced debriefing with may have the same problem." Open with the history — debriefing was standard practice for two decades before trials showed it could entrench symptoms — and then show PFA repeating the pattern. Grant Devilly at Griffith University is the obvious call; he has been arguing this for years and will be quotable. Be explicit that this is a lab stress-video analogue, not a disaster zone.
studies.wider_angle: A workplace and institutional story for a general-interest outlet: employers, schools and emergency services routinely deploy group debrief-style sessions after critical incidents. What does "stepped, individualized care" actually look like in an HR policy, and who is liable if the mandatory group session makes things worse?
studies.caveats: Small N (84 randomized, 74 completed); analogue distress-video paradigm rather than real trauma; self-reported outcomes only; two-week follow-up; single center; the harmful subgroup finding is an interaction in a small sample and needs replication.

studies.title: Nearly one in ten UK therapy clients says they recovered a memory of abuse they had not previously known about
studies.ns_score_reason: a nationally representative estimate of a practice most people assume died out in the 1990s, from clients rather than therapists.
studies.the_study: Lawrence Patihis surveyed a representative UK sample of 1,507 adults, 40% of whom had received therapy. Among the full sample, 4.9% said a therapist had discussed repressed memories of abuse with them (half the time the therapist raised it first), and 3.6% reported recovering memories during therapy of abuse they had not previously known about — 8.9% of everyone who had had therapy. Rates were highest for primal therapy, internal family systems and psychodynamic therapy, and were not confined to the 1980s: for therapy started between 2006 and 2024 the rate was 8–12%.
studies.why_it_matters: The recovered-memory debate is usually discussed in the past tense, and previous prevalence estimates came from therapists, who have obvious reasons to under-report. Asking clients directly suggests the practice is ongoing and affects millions of people in the UK.
studies.pitch_angle: "Repressed memory therapy never went away." Lead with the number — 8.9% of British therapy-goers — and the fact that rates are as high for therapy started in the last two decades as during the memory wars. Call Patihis (University of Portsmouth), and get a response from the UKCP or BACP on what current training says about memory construction. Handle carefully: the story is about how memory can be constructed under suggestion, not a claim that any individual's memories are false.
studies.wider_angle: A legal and forensic feature for a specialist or long-read outlet on how courts in the UK now treat testimony based on memories recovered in therapy, and how the science of reconsolidation and imagination inflation has and hasn't reached the justice system.
studies.caveats: Self-reported and retrospective — clients' accounts of what a therapist said may be imprecise; no verification of memory accuracy in either direction; therapy modality labels are client-reported; cross-sectional survey.

studies.title: People can track an object that has no visible features at all — a tiger defined only by the grass moving around it
studies.ns_score_reason: vivid, demonstrable, and it undercuts a core assumption of object-tracking models; it is basic vision science rather than health news.
studies.the_study: Across four experiments, observers watched grids of hundreds of small elements (for instance, randomly oriented crosses) in which an invisible "object" was defined purely by a propagating wave of change — each element switching to a new random orientation, brightness or shape as the object passed. Participants not only detected this second-order motion, they perceived it as a persisting object and could perform multiple-object tracking on several such objects at once, even when the type of change was haphazardly interleaved from element to element.
studies.why_it_matters: Standard models assume tracking works by continuously re-identifying an object's surface features across time; here there are no enduring features to re-identify, implying the visual system can bind "change itself" into an object.
studies.pitch_angle: "You can watch a tiger you cannot see." Lead with the demo — New Scientist could embed or describe the display — and the evolutionary framing the authors use: the most important objects are camouflaged ones. Brian Scholl's lab at Yale is the call, and Scholl is an unusually good explainer of phenomenological demonstrations.
studies.wider_angle: A technology feature for a computing or defense-adjacent outlet: machine vision systems track by feature re-identification and are systematically fooled by exactly this class of stimulus. What would a change-based tracker look like, and does biological vision have a trick worth stealing for camouflage detection?
studies.caveats: Sample sizes per experiment not reported in the abstract; laboratory display stimuli whose relation to real-world camouflage is an interpretation, not a test; no clinical or applied outcome.

studies.title: Working memory is not the main thing helping you understand speech in a noisy room — reasoning ability is
studies.ns_score_reason: directly challenges a dominant assumption in hearing research, with a clean multivariate design; N is modest and the study is online.
studies.the_study: Eighty-nine healthy adults listened to sentences degraded in five different ways and reported the words they heard, and also completed Reading Span and N-back tests of working memory plus a short form of Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices for fluid reasoning. All cognitive measures correlated with intelligibility on their own — but in multivariate and dominance analyses, fluid reasoning was clearly the strongest predictor, with working memory contributing little unique variance.
studies.why_it_matters: Decades of "listening effort" research and hearing-aid outcome prediction have leaned on working memory span, particularly the Reading Span test, as the cognitive resource that lets people decode degraded speech. This suggests the relevant ability is more general problem solving.
studies.pitch_angle: "Why some people cope in a noisy bar — it isn't memory." Open on the cocktail-party problem everyone recognizes, then explain that the standard cognitive explanation may have been an artifact of testing one construct at a time. Call Joseph Rovetti and Ingrid Johnsrude at Western University; Johnsrude is a central figure in the working-memory-and-hearing literature, which makes the result more interesting, not less.
studies.wider_angle: A specialist audiology/health-technology piece on what clinics actually measure when they predict who will benefit from hearing aids or cochlear implants, and whether a widely used cognitive screening battery is measuring the wrong thing.
studies.caveats: Small N (89) for an individual-differences study; online testing with uncontrolled listening conditions; healthy adults, not people with hearing loss; cross-sectional and correlational; short-form Raven's.

studies.title: The slowness of depression may be a timing prediction problem, not a movement problem
studies.ns_score_reason: a specific, testable reframing of psychomotor retardation with a striking frequency-specific signature; modest clinical sample.
studies.the_study: Thirty-eight people with major depressive disorder and 65 healthy controls tapped in time with rhythmic tone sequences at a range of tempos. Basic motor function — tapping speed, stability, interval production — was intact in the depressed group. What was disrupted was synchronization specifically below 1 Hz, the range corresponding to the motor system's natural delta rhythm, and the size of that desynchronization tracked depression severity, psychomotor anhedonia and vegetative symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: Psychomotor retardation is one of the oldest observed features of depression and has been treated as a motor output deficit; this locates it instead in the predictive timing signals the motor system sends to sensory areas, which is a cognitive mechanism with different treatment implications.
studies.pitch_angle: "Depression may slow you down by breaking your internal metronome." Open on the clinical observation — the slowed speech and movement clinicians have described for a century — then show the frequency-specific finding: only the slow rhythms break. Georg Northoff (University of Ottawa) is an excellent, quotable source on temporal structure in psychiatric disorders; Nai Ding at Zhejiang University for the auditory-motor rhythm science.
studies.wider_angle: A music-and-brain feature for a general-interest outlet on rhythm as a clinical tool: why rhythmic auditory cueing helps in Parkinson's, whether slow-tempo synchronization could ever serve as an objective marker of mood state, and what a "biomarker you can tap out with your finger" would mean for a field short of objective measures.
studies.caveats: Small N (38 patients); cross-sectional and correlational — cannot establish whether timing deficits cause or follow depressive symptoms; medication status not described in the abstract; unequal group sizes; single site.

studies.title: Insomnia, not oxygen starvation, explains the link between disturbed sleep and depression
studies.ns_score_reason: two harmonized population cohorts with objective sleep measurement, and a clean null for the mechanism most people assume; cross-sectional.
studies.the_study: Researchers harmonized two Australian and Swedish community cohorts (n=1,238; 68% male, mean age 57) with objective sleep recordings. Neither apnea-hypopnea index nor oxygen desaturation index was associated with depressive symptoms. Reduced sleep efficiency and increased wake after sleep onset were — but those associations disappeared once insomnia symptoms were added to the model.
studies.why_it_matters: Sleep apnea is routinely described as a cause of depression via intermittent hypoxia; in samples free of clinical referral bias, the depression signal seems to come from the subjective experience of broken sleep rather than from oxygen dips.
studies.pitch_angle: "Your CPAP machine may not be the thing standing between you and a better mood." Lead with the null on hypoxia, which is the mechanism most sleep-clinic patients are told about. Jenny Theorell-Haglöw at Uppsala and Nathaniel Marshall at the Woolcock Institute are the calls. Be careful to frame this as observational and cross-sectional — no advice on treatment decisions.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health outlet on the widening gulf between "objective" and "felt" sleep: people whose polysomnography looks fine but who feel wrecked, the growing recognition of insomnia as a distinct disorder rather than a symptom, and why the two are treated by different specialties.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional design — cannot establish causation or direction; depressive and insomnia symptoms both self-reported, raising shared-method concerns; two cohorts differ by sex composition (one all-women, one all-men) and were harmonized post hoc; middle-aged and older community samples may not generalize to younger people or clinical apnea populations.

studies.title: Reminding older people of the "memory decline" stereotype doesn't wreck their recall — it makes them study for longer
studies.ns_score_reason: a nuanced, partially null result in a literature under replication pressure; small sample keeps the score down.
studies.the_study: Ninety-two older adults were randomized to a stereotype threat condition or a control condition and completed a self-paced word-pair learning task with judgments of learning. Threat had no significant effect on how well people predicted their own learning, on the accuracy of those predictions, or on how they distributed study time across easy and hard items. What it did change was total study time: threatened participants spent longer studying and had to mobilize extra effort to reach the same performance as controls.
studies.why_it_matters: Stereotype threat in aging is usually framed as a performance-destroying phenomenon; here the cost shows up as reduced processing efficiency — the same result achieved for more effort — which is a subtler and arguably more realistic account of what negative age stereotypes do.
studies.pitch_angle: "Ageism doesn't make you forget — it makes you work harder for the same result." Open on the moment of being handed a memory test after being told memory declines with age. Lucie Guerrero and Badiâa Bouazzaoui are the calls, and they can speak to why the metamemory effects everyone expected didn't appear. Situate it in the broader replication debate around stereotype threat.
studies.wider_angle: A workplace or economics angle for a general-interest outlet: if age stereotypes tax cognitive resources rather than degrading output, the cost is invisible in performance metrics and shows up instead as fatigue — with implications for how older workers are assessed and how "cognitive load" is measured at work.
studies.caveats: Small N (92); laboratory word-pair task with uncertain relevance to everyday memory; single center; several key results are null, so the positive study-time finding needs replication.

studies.title: Most children in mental health services report feeling watched or followed — and no one is asking about it
studies.ns_score_reason: first data on "felt presence" in young people, with a striking prevalence figure; exploratory, and the authors say their own measure was inadequate.
studies.the_study: Within the ChUSE feasibility RCT in NHS Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services, 50 young people aged 8–16 reported on distressing sensory experiences at baseline. Feeling watched or followed was reported by 88%, and 28% said it was the experience that distressed them most. Among those who went on to receive therapy in the trial, 63.8% described regularly experiencing a felt presence and being distressed by it.
studies.why_it_matters: Felt presence — the sense that someone unseen is nearby — is a well-documented phenomenon in adults with psychosis, Parkinson's and sleep paralysis, but has never been studied in children in clinical care; if these rates hold up, routine assessment is missing something common and highly distressing.
studies.pitch_angle: "The invisible person in the room: the childhood experience clinicians never ask about." Open on a young person describing a presence at the end of the bed, then the number: 88%. Ben Alderson-Day at Durham has written a book on felt presence and is a strong interviewee; Sarah Parry can speak to the CAMHS side. The honest framing is that this opens a line of enquiry, not that it changes practice yet.
studies.wider_angle: A cultural-science feature for a magazine or podcast on felt presence across contexts — sleep paralysis, mountaineers' "third man", bereavement, Parkinson's — and what a single phenomenon appearing under so many conditions tells us about how the brain models other minds and bodies in space.
studies.caveats: Small N (50); no control group of non-clinical young people, so the 88% figure cannot be interpreted as elevated; the authors explicitly flag that their assessment of felt presence was not a validated measure; sample not diverse; single trial embedded in a feasibility study.

studies.title: Sitting through a criminal trial did not make bereaved relatives' grief worse — or better
studies.ns_score_reason: a well-powered longitudinal null in an extraordinary natural experiment; null results are harder to sell but this one has a strong hook.
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 237 people bereaved by the shooting down of flight MH17 across the criminal trial of the perpetrators, using longitudinal confirmatory factor analysis. Prolonged grief and mental well-being emerged as distinct, negatively related constructs whose relationship stayed stable over time — and neither predicted the other over time. Crucially, no aspect of criminal justice system involvement was associated with grief or well-being levels after the trial, once pre-trial levels were accounted for.
studies.why_it_matters: Both the "therapeutic jurisprudence" literature and the popular idea of "closure" assume that participation in a trial materially changes bereaved people's mental health. In this cohort it did neither, and grief and well-being turn out to be two separate dials rather than opposite ends of one.
studies.pitch_angle: "Closure is a myth — a landmark trial changed nothing about relatives' grief." Open on the MH17 courtroom in the Netherlands, then the data. Lonneke Lenferink at Twente/Groningen is the call. The second finding is the more useful one for readers: reducing grief and building well-being appear to be separate therapeutic tasks.
studies.wider_angle: A justice-system feature for a legal or general-interest outlet on victim impact statements and the promises courts make to bereaved families — what victims actually say they want from a trial, and whether the mental health rationale for expanded victim participation is supported by evidence.
studies.caveats: Observational; a single, highly unusual mass-casualty event with unusually strong state support for the bereaved, which limits generalization; the perpetrators were tried in absentia; self-reported measures; null findings on CJS involvement need replication before informing policy.

studies.title: How much you'd be blamed for *not* doing something predicts your behavior better than how much you'd be praised for doing it
studies.ns_score_reason: a simple conceptual reframe that predicts real behavior including actual voting, across six studies; the moral-psychology framing needs work for a general audience.
studies.the_study: Across six studies, the authors argue that moral acts carry two separable evaluations — praise for doing them (virtue) and blame for not doing them (duty) — and that these are not systematically related to each other. Measuring both improved predictions of intended blood donation and of actual voting behavior, and helped explain two puzzles: why Republicans masked less than Democrats during COVID-19, and why paying people for blood reduces donation.
studies.why_it_matters: Public health and civic campaigns routinely choose between praising good behavior and shaming its absence; this suggests those are independent levers, and that the wrong one can be pulled — paying for blood, for example, appears to strip an act of its duty status.
studies.pitch_angle: "Why paying people to give blood makes them give less." Lead with the blood donation paradox, which readers find genuinely strange, then unpack the virtue/duty distinction and the mask-wearing result. Julian Zlatev at Harvard Business School and Dale Miller at Stanford are the calls; ask whether the framework predicts anything about recycling, tax compliance or vaccination.
studies.wider_angle: A behavioral-policy feature for a business or politics outlet on why "nudge" campaigns keep misfiring on politically coded behaviors, and what happens when a government tries to convert a virtue into a duty (or vice versa) — mask mandates, mandatory voting, organ donation opt-out.
studies.caveats: Multiple studies but sample sizes and populations not specified in the abstract; likely online panel samples with limited generalization; some outcomes are intentions rather than behavior; the COVID masking explanation is post hoc.

studies.title: Brain waves recorded a week after a stroke predict who will still be recovering thinking skills six months later
studies.ns_score_reason: prospective design and a good discrimination statistic, but a single-center cohort under 100 with a surprising direction of effect that needs external validation.
studies.the_study: Ninety-six patients with a first mild-to-moderate ischemic stroke had resting EEG recorded around eight days after the event, then MoCA cognitive testing at three and six months. Just over half (55.2%) showed meaningful cognitive recovery. Counterintuitively, *lower* frontal peak alpha frequency and *reduced* frontal slow-to-fast wave ratio predicted recovery, alongside elevated frontal frequency variability, together discriminating recoverers with an AUC of 0.831. Recoverers looked worse at three months but caught up by six.
studies.why_it_matters: Post-stroke cognitive impairment affects 30–60% of survivors and rehabilitation is often withdrawn early on the basis of a poor three-month assessment; if early EEG can flag late bloomers, some patients are being written off too soon.
studies.pitch_angle: "The stroke patients who look worst at three months are often the ones still improving." Lead with the clinical decision point — when do you stop rehab? — and the fact that the EEG markers predicted recovery in the opposite direction to what a "healthier brain recovers better" intuition suggests. Tran Cong Thang and Nguyen Van Tuan at Ho Chi Minh City are the calls; a Western stroke rehabilitation researcher for independent assessment.
studies.wider_angle: A health-technology piece for a specialist or general outlet on the quiet revival of EEG — cheap, portable, decades old — as a prognostic tool in an era of expensive imaging, and what it would take for a low-cost bedside test to change rehabilitation funding decisions.
studies.caveats: Small N (96) and single center; observational cohort — no test of whether acting on the prediction improves outcomes; recovery defined by a 2-point MoCA change, a fairly coarse threshold; predictors selected by stepwise regression in the same sample, risking overfitting; no external validation cohort; Vietnamese sample may not generalize.

studies.title: Men and women's prolonged grief hangs together differently — identity loss is more central for men
studies.ns_score_reason: large sample and a clear, humanly recognizable result, but network analysis findings are notoriously unstable and this is cross-sectional.
studies.the_study: A total of 1,093 bereaved adults in Hong Kong (274 men; mean age 37) completed the PG-13-Revised, and the authors compared symptom networks by gender. Women reported more severe symptoms overall, but the overall connectivity of the networks was similar. What differed was structure: "meaninglessness" and "disengagement" were the most central symptoms for both genders, while "identity disruption" — not knowing who you are without the person — was significantly more central in men.
studies.why_it_matters: Grief is usually characterized by severity; this suggests the architecture of grief differs by gender, and that men's grief may hinge disproportionately on a loss of self rather than on longing.
studies.pitch_angle: "Men's grief has a different shape." Open on a widower describing not knowing who he is anymore, then the network finding. Amy Chow at the University of Hong Kong runs the Jockey Club bereavement alliance and is well placed to talk about what gender-sensitive grief support would actually involve. Flag that men were only a quarter of the sample.
studies.wider_angle: A social feature for a general-interest outlet on the collapse of men's social networks in midlife, and why bereavement support services — overwhelmingly used by women — struggle to reach bereaved men at all.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional; men were only 25% of the sample, which affects the precision of network comparisons; single cultural context (Hong Kong) with unclear generalization; self-reported symptoms; the functional impairment analyses are explicitly exploratory; network centrality estimates are known to be sensitive to sample and item selection.

studies.title: The brain's waste-clearance system looks more impaired in people on two antipsychotics than one
studies.ns_score_reason: a novel and clinically pointed observation about a very common prescribing pattern, but small, cross-sectional, and using a proxy measure of glymphatic function.
studies.the_study: Using diffusion tensor imaging along perivascular spaces (the DTI-ALPS index, a non-invasive proxy for glymphatic clearance), researchers compared 37 patients with chronic schizophrenia on risperidone plus clozapine, 30 on risperidone alone and 36 healthy controls. Both patient groups had lower ALPS indices than controls, and the combination-therapy group was lower still, particularly in the left hemisphere. Lower ALPS values correlated with worse cognitive performance.
studies.why_it_matters: Antipsychotic polypharmacy is widespread and poorly evidenced; if it is associated with reduced clearance of brain waste, that offers a candidate mechanism for the cognitive costs clinicians have long suspected — though causal direction is entirely unresolved here.
studies.pitch_angle: "Does taking two antipsychotics clog the brain's drainage system?" Pair this with the Hong Kong polypharmacy trend data (entry 15) for a single, richer piece: prescribing of two-drug combinations is rising while evidence for it stays thin. Nian Liu's group at North Sichuan Medical College is the call; a glymphatic researcher such as someone from the Nedergaard lab would be needed to assess how much the DTI-ALPS index can really tell us. Do not imply anyone should change medication.
studies.wider_angle: A neuroscience feature for a specialist outlet on how quickly the glymphatic system has gone from a 2012 discovery in mice to a routinely reported human imaging index — and whether DTI-ALPS actually measures what its users claim.
studies.caveats: Small N per group; cross-sectional and observational — patients on combination therapy are by definition more treatment-resistant, which could drive both the imaging and the cognitive findings; DTI-ALPS is an indirect proxy for glymphatic function and is contested; single center; no illness-duration or dose matching described in the abstract.

studies.title: Antipsychotic polypharmacy is rising again, 21 years of prescribing records show
studies.ns_score_reason: territory-wide data over two decades is unusually solid, but it is a descriptive trend paper without an individual-level hook.
studies.the_study: Using electronic health records for every adult diagnosed with schizophrenia in Hong Kong from 2004 to 2024, researchers tracked prescribing. Overall antipsychotic use barely moved, but the mix changed dramatically: second-generation drugs overtook first-generation, olanzapine became the most prescribed single agent (20.6% in 2024), and clozapine use grew but stayed low at 7.5%. Polypharmacy fell from 24.0% in 2004 to 22.4% in 2011, then climbed to 28.0% by 2024.
studies.why_it_matters: Guidelines have discouraged combining antipsychotics for decades and encouraged clozapine for treatment-resistant illness; this shows the opposite happening in a whole health system, with more than a quarter of patients on multiple agents.
studies.pitch_angle: Best used as the data spine of the combination-therapy story with entry 14: guidelines say one drug, and clozapine when one fails; real-world practice is drifting the other way. Esther Chan at the University of Hong Kong is the call, plus a UK or Australian prescribing researcher to say whether the pattern holds outside Hong Kong.
studies.wider_angle: A health-systems piece for a policy or medical outlet on why clozapine — the only drug with strong evidence in treatment-resistant schizophrenia — remains stubbornly underused worldwide, and what its monitoring requirements cost patients in outcomes.
studies.caveats: Descriptive prescribing data with no outcome measures — says nothing about whether polypharmacy helped or harmed; single jurisdiction; an erratum has already been published for this paper; several authors report consulting and research funding from industry (declared as unrelated), including funding from Amgen and GSK to one author.

studies.title: Insecure attachment predicts avoiding conversations about sexual consent
studies.ns_score_reason: moves consent research from social norms to individual psychology, which is genuinely new, but this is a first model test with mixed support.
studies.the_study: The authors propose the Integrative Cognitive-Affective Model of Sexual Consent Communication, in which attachment insecurity undermines consent communication through two routes: reduced mentalizing (reading the other person's mind) and poor emotion regulation, which makes people perceive consent conversations as costly. In a sample of 395 participants completing measures of all key constructs, attachment insecurity, mentalizing and emotion regulation did predict consent motivations and behavior — although several pathways ran differently than predicted.
studies.why_it_matters: Consent education is built almost entirely on norms, scripts and social context; this suggests some people find these conversations hard for reasons rooted in how they learned to do intimacy, which would call for a different kind of intervention.
studies.pitch_angle: "Why some people can't have the conversation." Open on the gap between knowing you should ask and being able to, then the attachment mechanism. Jessica Edwards and Uzma Rehman at the University of Waterloo are the calls; ask them directly which hypothesized pathways failed and what that means for the model. Frame as preliminary theory-testing, not as advice.
studies.wider_angle: An education feature for a general-interest or higher-education outlet on what a decade of campus consent programs has and hasn't achieved, and whether emotion-regulation and mentalizing skills — the stuff of therapy, not workshops — belong in the curriculum.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, self-reported, single sample (N=395, likely a student or online convenience sample); the authors themselves note several pathways diverged from the model and that alternative pathways were not tested; no behavioral or dyadic data.

studies.title: Autistic adults say talking to non-autistic people costs more effort — and noise makes them lose words
studies.ns_score_reason: a decent-sized survey putting numbers and first-person description behind the double empathy problem; self-report and retrospective.
studies.the_study: Using the Neurotype Communication and Assistive Technology Survey, researchers collected quantitative ratings and written descriptions from 154 autistic adults aged 18–35 about past conversations. Most said environmental factors — crowding, noise, unfamiliarity — affected their communication, with noisy or unpredictable settings producing word loss, scripting and withdrawal. Conversations with non-autistic partners were consistently described as requiring more conscious effort, masking and cognitive load than conversations with other autistic people. Negative emotions worsened communication regardless of who they were speaking to.
studies.why_it_matters: The double empathy problem — the idea that autistic communication difficulty is a two-way mismatch, not a one-way deficit — has been influential but thinly evidenced; this adds first-person data and identifies environment and emotional state as separate, modifiable factors.
studies.pitch_angle: "Autistic adults find it easier to talk to each other — and here's what the room has to do with it." Lead with the specific, vivid detail of losing words in a noisy café. Zachary Miller (Michigan State) and Carla Mazefsky (Pittsburgh) are the calls. The practical angle — quiet rooms, predictable settings — is concrete without overclaiming.
studies.wider_angle: A design and architecture feature for a general-interest outlet on sensory design in offices, hospitals and schools: open-plan environments were built on a theory of collaboration that appears to disable a substantial minority of workers.
studies.caveats: Self-reported and retrospective reflections rather than observed conversations; convenience sample recruited online, likely skewed toward diagnosed, verbally fluent adults aged 18–35; no non-autistic comparison group; cross-sectional.

studies.title: Mental fatigue and physical fatigue push you off the sofa in completely different ways
studies.ns_score_reason: a three-month longitudinal design with a clean dissociation, though half the paper is a scale validation and outcomes are self-reported.
studies.the_study: In a two-part study, researchers validated an Italian version of the Physical Effort Scale (675 participants), then followed 424 adults (mean age 25) over three months. Physical fatigue predicted lower physical activity indirectly, by reducing the tendency to approach physical effort and increasing the tendency to avoid it — an effect strongest for vigorous activity. Mental fatigue had no relationship with those approach/avoidance tendencies at all, but directly predicted less light and moderate activity.
studies.why_it_matters: Public health messaging treats "too tired to exercise" as one thing; these data suggest tired body and tired brain suppress activity through separate routes, meaning the same motivational intervention would not work for both.
studies.pitch_angle: "Two kinds of tired, two reasons you skipped the gym." Open on the after-work decision point, then the dissociation: physical fatigue changes how you feel about effort, mental fatigue just quietly removes your walking and light activity. Boris Cheval (ENS Rennes) is the standout call — he works on the theory that humans are wired to avoid unnecessary effort.
studies.wider_angle: A workplace-health feature for a business or general outlet on the cognitive cost of desk work: if mental fatigue selectively erodes light and moderate activity — walking, stairs, chores — then knowledge work may be depleting exactly the movement that matters most for long-term health.
studies.caveats: Self-reported physical activity throughout; young sample (mean age 25) recruited in Italy, limiting generalization; observational and mediational — the causal ordering is assumed, not tested experimentally; Study 1 is a scale validation with limited news value on its own.

studies.title: Precision psychiatry audit: only a handful of tools are ready for the clinic
studies.ns_score_reason: a narrative review rather than new data, but the readiness triage is a useful spine for a skeptical trend piece.
studies.the_study: The authors applied a structured framework — validity, external replication, incremental utility, actionability, patient benefit, feasibility, equity, governance — to the major approaches under the banner of precision psychiatry. Only structured longitudinal measurement-based care, therapeutic drug monitoring for selected drugs, and a few pharmacogenetic gene-drug pairs qualified as clinically actionable. Digital phenotyping, AI decision support, neuroimaging and blood biomarkers were "promising but not ready". Polygenic risk scores, multiomic subtyping, diagnostic neuroimaging, automated treatment selection and automated suicide prediction were classed as experimental.
studies.why_it_matters: Direct-to-consumer pharmacogenetic tests and AI mental health prediction tools are already being sold; this puts a structured, criterion-based judgment on what the evidence actually supports.
studies.pitch_angle: A reported piece rather than a study write-up: use the readiness ladder as the structure and go to the companies selling the experimental tier — particularly pharmacogenetic panels and automated suicide risk prediction — for their evidence. Julio Torales and Antonio Ventriglio for the framework; a critic of polygenic risk scoring in psychiatry for balance.
studies.wider_angle: A health-technology investigation for a specialist outlet on suicide risk prediction algorithms now deployed in health systems and social media platforms, and the accountability gap the authors flag: nobody has settled who is responsible when an automated prediction is wrong.
studies.caveats: Narrative review, not systematic — inclusion and classification decisions are the authors' judgment; no new data; readiness categories are inherently subjective and will date quickly.

studies.title: Working memory chunks the world differently depending on what marks the boundaries
studies.ns_score_reason: solid four-experiment work on a mechanism everyone has heard of (chunking), but the representational-geometry framing is hard to make vivid.
studies.the_study: Across four behavioral experiments, participants encoded nine-item sequences and later reported an item's original position. Sequences varied in how strongly chunk boundaries were signaled: structured linguistic sequences produced a near-orthogonal representation, with clearly separable "which chunk" and "where in the chunk" codes. Color-segmented shapes gave a weaker, partially collapsed version. Scrambled sequences and uniformly colored shapes collapsed entirely to a single dimension.
studies.why_it_matters: Chunking is textbook — the reason phone numbers are grouped — but this shows it does not produce one uniform format; whether you get a genuinely two-level positional code depends on the strength of the boundary cue.
studies.pitch_angle: "Why grouping a phone number only helps if the gaps are obvious enough." Lead with the everyday memory trick, then the finding that weak boundary cues give you the appearance of chunking without the underlying structure. Lin Zhan at Beijing Language and Culture University is the call. This works best as a short front-of-book piece.
studies.wider_angle: An interface-design story for a technology outlet on how information is grouped in passwords, one-time codes, addresses and form fields — and whether current conventions supply strong enough boundary cues to actually help memory.
studies.caveats: Sample sizes not given in the abstract; laboratory sequence-memory task; the group-level "intermediate" result partly reflects individual heterogeneity, which the authors acknowledge; language-specific stimuli may limit generalization.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**

- **Popular psychological interventions keep failing when properly tested.** The new batch's "Relaxation exercises may make some talk therapies work less well" (PMID 42546730) and "Psychological first aid after trauma performs worse than doing nothing" (PMID 42561812) extend a pattern already strong in the previous digest: mindfulness did not buffer discrimination in Black mothers (PMID 42622844), mindfulness failed to protect tweens against problematic social media use (PMID 42612528), symptom reframing produced no effect in somatic symptom disorder (PMID 42629541), and intensive self-monitoring changed nothing in alcohol recovery (PMID 42606857). Two runs in a row, the null and negative results are landing on exactly the interventions most heavily promoted to the public.
- **Real-world antipsychotic prescribing keeps drifting away from guidelines.** "Antipsychotic polypharmacy is rising again" (PMID 42551239) and the glymphatic imaging study of dual antipsychotics (PMID 42551238) sit directly alongside the previous digest's finding that one in five clozapine prescriptions worldwide is off-label (PMID 42628494). Both runs describe whole-system prescribing data showing guidelines and practice diverging, with clozapine underused in one and misapplied in the other.
- **Cheap EEG as a prognostic tool, with counterintuitive directions of effect.** "Brain waves recorded a week after a stroke predict who will still be recovering" (PMID 42663449) mirrors the previous run's gamma-band signature in early-onset Alzheimer's (PMID 42617666): both are small, single-center cohorts, both report an inverted expectation (worse-looking signal predicts better outcome; more gamma, not less), and both land near an AUC of 0.83. The recurring caution is the same — no external validation.

**Advances**

- **From whole packages to active ingredients.** The previous digest's mediation analysis of video-feedback parenting (PMID 42613957) asked which mechanism carried an intervention's effect; the new component network meta-analysis of 10,612 patients (PMID 42546730) does this at scale and across 30 trials, and finds some ingredients pulling in the wrong direction. This is the same research program a generation on in ambition.
- **Autism coverage moves from counting to lived experience.** The previous run's England-wide identification data (PMID 42613816) documented a doubling in prevalence and a narrowing sex gap; the new survey of 154 autistic adults on communication effort and noise (PMID 42547992) speaks to what that larger, more diverse identified population actually needs from rooms, workplaces and conversations.

**Counterpoints**

- **Algorithmic suicide risk prediction.** The previous digest's narrative review proposed a connectome-based suicide risk calculator (PMID 42612815) and reported clinicians warming to the probability-based OxSATS score (PMID 42618280). The new precision psychiatry readiness audit (PMID 42657684) classifies automated suicide prediction, neuroimaging diagnostics and polygenic scores as experimental, and flags an unresolved accountability gap — a direct brake on the optimism of both earlier items.
- **Oxygen as a lever on the brain.** The previous run tested low-oxygen air as a circadian intervention and found a non-significant shift (PMID 42630089); the new cohort analysis finds oxygen desaturation unrelated to depressive symptoms once insomnia is accounted for (PMID 42663413). Same journal, opposite ends of the same assumption that hypoxia is a meaningful lever on mood and rhythm.

**New themes**

- **Grief as a structured, measurable thing rather than a mood.** Two European Journal of Psychotraumatology papers — the MH17 trial cohort showing no effect of criminal justice involvement (PMID 42635331) and the gendered symptom network in Hong Kong (PMID 42635333) — open a topic absent from the previous digest.
- **Iatrogenic risk inside therapy itself.** "Nearly one in ten UK therapy clients says they recovered a memory of abuse" (PMID 42663614) has no analogue in the previous run and shifts the frame from "does therapy work" to "what does therapy do to people."
- **Basic cognition returns.** Tracking a featureless object (PMID 42537447), reasoning rather than working memory predicting speech-in-noise (PMID 42659749), and chunk-boundary geometry in working memory (PMID 42552609) restore a strand of pure cognitive science that the previous, health-heavy batch lacked.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Several studies in this batch converge on the idea that psychological interventions have active ingredients, inert ingredients and adverse effects — and that hardly anyone measures the last two. A component analysis of more than 10,000 patients finds relaxation training and cognitive reframing associated with worse outcomes while social support does the heavy lifting (PMID 42546730); a randomized test of psychological first aid finds it slowed recovery, with the most distressed participants worse off two weeks later (PMID 42561812); nearly one in ten UK therapy clients reports recovering a previously unknown memory of abuse in the consulting room (PMID 42663614); the "closure" that courts promise bereaved families did nothing measurable across the MH17 trial (PMID 42635331); and a structured readiness audit finds only a handful of precision psychiatry tools clinically actionable (PMID 42657684).

**Why pitch this now:** Task-shared therapy, app-delivered relaxation modules and mandatory post-incident debriefs are being scaled globally on the assumption that psychological help is at worst neutral — and this batch is the first time the evidence against that assumption has arrived from several independent directions at once.

**Angle:** A reported feature on psychology's missing side-effect register: what it would take to treat therapies like drug formularies, with named components, doses and adverse event reporting, written for readers who have sat through a workplace debrief, downloaded a breathing app or been handed a therapy referral and assumed the worst case was that it wouldn't help.

**Potential headlines:**
- Some parts of talk therapy make patients worse, and trials are starting to say which
- The most soothing bits of therapy are the ones failing their tests
- Psychology has never kept a side-effect register, and patients are paying for it

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the Mind section already runs component-level and "does therapy work" pieces, and the Lancet Psychiatry dataset gives the feature a quantitative spine rather than a therapy-culture essay.
- **The Atlantic** — has an established readership for critical writing about therapy's cultural authority; the recovered-memory prevalence figure and the debrief history give it narrative stakes.
- **STAT** — the prescribing, readiness-audit and task-shared delivery threads are squarely clinical-policy territory, and STAT's audience will care about who owns adverse-event reporting for a psychosocial intervention.
- **Undark** — well suited to the accountability angle: interventions rolled out worldwide on weak evidence, and the institutions that never asked for harm data.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — August 2026
**Checked:** 2026-08-28 | **Studies reviewed:** 20
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-08-28

---

### Study 1: Relaxation exercises may make some talk therapies work less well, huge patient-level analysis finds
**PMID:** 42546730 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Core numbers check out: 30 trials contributing IPD from 10,612 participants (72.2% women, mean age 36.7), social support −9.48, behavioural activation −4.15, problem management −4.08, relaxation +7.97, cognitive reframing +5.17 ("less clearly" detrimental in the abstract, which the digest reflects as "also on the detrimental side"). Funding (European Commission) and the Furukawa app/pharma disclosures are correctly carried into Caveats.

**Issue A. Funder misattributed in wider angle** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "and what a WHO-funded personalization web app means for delivering mental health care in countries with almost no psychiatrists."
- **Abstract says:** "FUNDING: European Commission." / "Personalised effect estimates can be computed via a freely accessible web application."
- **Problem:** The digest's own Caveats correctly say the study was funded by the European Commission, but the wider angle calls the web app "WHO-funded". Several authors sit at WHO Collaborating Centres and one is WHO staff, but that is not the same as WHO funding, and the abstract states a different funder. An editor pitched on this would print a wrong funder.
- **Suggested fix:** "and what a freely accessible personalisation web app, from a European Commission-funded team working with WHO collaborating centres, means for delivering mental health care in countries with almost no psychiatrists."

**Issue B. Trial settings not verifiable from the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "trials were largely in low-resource and humanitarian settings, so generalization to specialist Western care is uncertain"
- **Abstract says:** Describes only "task-shared psychosocial interventions… delivered by non-specialist providers" for "adults with common mental disorders"; no breakdown of trial settings is given.
- **Problem:** The task-shared/non-specialist framing is supported, but "largely in low-resource and humanitarian settings" (and the same claim in the pitch angle) is Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "trials tested task-shared delivery by non-specialist providers, so generalisation to specialist Western care is uncertain (check the included-trial table for the setting mix before pitching)."

---

### Study 2: Psychological first aid after trauma performs worse than doing nothing in a randomized trial
**PMID:** 42561812 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N (84; PFA 47, control 37; 74 completing follow-up), the medium-effect-size immediate advantage for controls, the null at two weeks, and the high-initial-distress interaction are all accurately reported.

**Issue A. Headline implies real trauma exposure** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Psychological first aid after trauma performs worse than doing nothing in a randomized trial"
- **Abstract says:** "This randomised controlled trial examined the efficacy of PFA compared to natural recovery in reducing psychological distress using a validated stress-video paradigm."
- **Problem:** The Caveats and pitch both correctly flag the analogue paradigm, but the headline says "after trauma", which readers will take to mean real traumatic incidents. The headline also flattens a mixed result (worse immediately, no difference at two weeks except in a subgroup) into a blanket "performs worse".
- **Suggested fix:** "Psychological first aid did worse than natural recovery in a lab trauma-video trial"

**Issue B. NS fit score high for the evidence base** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 8/10 — a randomized test of one of the world's most widely promoted post-disaster interventions, with a genuinely uncomfortable result; limited by the analogue stress paradigm."
- **Abstract says:** 84 randomised, 74 completed, self-report distress measures, analogue stress-video paradigm, single group-PFA protocol.
- **Problem:** Randomisation is a genuine strength, but the headline-grabbing element (harm in the most distressed) is an interaction in a subgroup of a sample under 100, with self-report outcomes and no real trauma exposure. An 8 implies more evidential weight than this design can carry.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — a randomised test of a globally promoted intervention with an uncomfortable result, but an 84-person analogue paradigm with self-reported outcomes and a subgroup-level harm signal."

---

### Study 3: Nearly one in ten UK therapy clients says they recovered a memory of abuse they had not previously known about
**PMID:** 42663614 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=1,507, 40% therapy uptake, 4.9% / 3.6% of the total sample, 8.9% of therapy-goers, modality ranking, and the 2006–2024 range of 8–12% all match. The "millions in the UK" phrasing tracks the authors' own wording.

**Issue A. 1980s comparison not supported by a reported figure** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and the fact that rates are as high for therapy started in the last two decades as during the memory wars"
- **Abstract says:** "Higher rates of memory recovery in therapy occurred when therapy started in the 1980s and recent decades (2006-2024: 8-12%)."
- **Problem:** The abstract gives a figure only for 2006–2024; no 1980s rate is reported, so an explicit equivalence claim between the two eras cannot be checked. The body text's weaker claim ("were not confined to the 1980s") is fine.
- **Suggested fix:** "and the fact that rates were also elevated for therapy started in recent decades, not just in the 1980s heyday of the memory wars"

---

### Study 4: People can track an object that has no visible features at all — a tiger defined only by the grass moving around it
**PMID:** 42537447 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Four experiments, the change-defined object construction, second-order motion detection, multiple-object tracking, generalisation to brightness/shape and to haphazardly interleaved change types are all correctly described, and the Caveat that per-experiment sample sizes are absent from the abstract is correct.

---

### Study 5: Working memory is not the main thing helping you understand speech in a noisy room — reasoning ability is
**PMID:** 42659749 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=89, five degradation types, Reading Span, N-back, short-form Raven's, bivariate correlations for all measures, and fluid reasoning as top predictor in multivariate/dominance analyses are accurate. The online design is correctly flagged.

**Issue A. Headline states as settled what the authors hedge** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Working memory is not the main thing helping you understand speech in a noisy room — reasoning ability is"
- **Abstract says:** "These results may undermine the assumption that WM, as measured by the Reading Span and other tasks, is the primary cognitive construct supporting degraded speech intelligibility."
- **Problem:** The abstract says "may undermine"; the headline asserts the reversal flatly. "In a noisy room" also narrows to one of five degradation types.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reasoning, not working memory, may be what helps you follow degraded speech"

**Issue B. Unique-variance claim not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "fluid reasoning was clearly the strongest predictor, with working memory contributing little unique variance"
- **Abstract says:** "multivariate and dominance analyses revealed that the test of fluid reasoning was the most important predictor of intelligibility."
- **Problem:** "Most important predictor" is reported; the specific claim that WM added little unique variance is a plausible inference but not stated. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "fluid reasoning was the most important predictor, ranking above both working memory measures"

---

### Study 6: The slowness of depression may be a timing prediction problem, not a movement problem
**PMID:** 42542090 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=38 MDD / 65 controls, intact basic motor function, frequency-specific desynchronisation below 1 Hz in the delta range, and correlations with depression severity, psychomotor anhedonia and vegetative symptoms are all accurate. Causal language is appropriately hedged ("may be", "tracked").

**Issue A. NS fit score high for sample size** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — a specific, testable reframing of psychomotor retardation with a striking frequency-specific signature; modest clinical sample."
- **Abstract says:** "We tested MDD subjects' (N = 38) ability to synchronize finger taps to rhythmic tone sequences… compared with healthy controls (N = 65)."
- **Problem:** A single-site, cross-sectional 38-patient study proposing a new mechanism for a century-old clinical feature, with medication status unreported, is thin support for a 7. The finding is objective rather than self-reported, which argues against dropping it further.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — a specific, testable reframing with a striking frequency-specific signature, but only 38 patients at a single site and no replication."

---

### Study 7: Insomnia, not oxygen starvation, explains the link between disturbed sleep and depression
**PMID:** 42663413 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

n=1,238, 68% male, mean age 57, the SHE (women) and MAILES (men) cohorts, the null for AHI and ODI, the significant SE% and WASO associations and their attenuation after adjusting for insomnia are all correct. The pitch explicitly instructs against treatment advice, which is the right call.

**Issue A. Headline uses explanatory language for a cross-sectional null** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Insomnia, not oxygen starvation, explains the link between disturbed sleep and depression"
- **Abstract says:** "While sleep fragmentation was associated with depressive symptoms, insomnia symptoms appear to be a key factor." (cross-sectional analysis; adjustment attenuates rather than establishes mechanism)
- **Problem:** "Explains" implies a mechanism established over time; this is a single cross-sectional adjustment in which associations lost significance, and depressive and insomnia symptoms share a self-report method. The body and Caveats hedge properly, so only the headline needs work.
- **Suggested fix:** "Insomnia symptoms, not low oxygen, may account for the link between disturbed sleep and depression"

---

### Study 8: Reminding older people of the "memory decline" stereotype doesn't wreck their recall — it makes them study for longer
**PMID:** 42554651 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N=92, random assignment, the three null results (JOL predictions, JOL accuracy, study-time adjustment by difficulty), the higher overall study time in the threatened group, and the "same performance for more resources" interpretation all match the abstract. Framing is consistent.

---

### Study 9: Most children in mental health services report feeling watched or followed — and no one is asking about it
**PMID:** 42658756 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The numbers (50 young people aged 8–16, 88%, 28%, 63.8%) are all accurate.

**Issue A. Population overgeneralised beyond a pre-selected trial sample** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Most children in mental health services report feeling watched or followed" / "50 young people aged 8–16 reported on distressing sensory experiences at baseline"
- **Abstract says:** "the experiences of FPs from a clinical sample of young people involved in the ChUSE trial, a feasibility and acceptability RCT looking at supporting young people with distressing sensory experiences (DSEs) within CAMHS services in the NHS."
- **Problem:** These 50 were recruited *because* they had distressing sensory experiences. The 88% therefore describes a highly selected subgroup, not children in CAMHS generally. The Caveats flag the absence of a non-clinical comparison group but not this selection step, and the headline generalises to all children in mental health services.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "Most young people in a trial for distressing sensory experiences report feeling watched or followed". Body: "Within the ChUSE feasibility RCT, 50 young people aged 8–16 who were already reporting distressing sensory experiences in NHS CAMHS reported on those experiences at baseline."

**Issue B. "No one is asking about it" overstates the authors' claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and no one is asking about it"
- **Abstract says:** "FPs are potentially more common and distressing for young people in CAMHS than previously recognised and routine assessment should be considered alongside assessment of other DSEs."
- **Problem:** The authors say routine assessment "should be considered" and that felt presence is under-recognised — not that clinicians never ask. The digest's own pitch note ("opens a line of enquiry") is more accurate than the headline.
- **Suggested fix:** "— and it is rarely asked about routinely"

---

### Study 10: Sitting through a criminal trial did not make bereaved relatives' grief worse — or better
**PMID:** 42635331 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=237, longitudinal CFA, PGD and well-being as distinct and negatively related constructs stable over time, neither predicting the other, and the null for CJS involvement after adjusting for pre-trial levels are all accurately reported.

**Issue A. Pitch headline overclaims from a single null** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "**Pitch angle:** "Closure is a myth — a landmark trial changed nothing about relatives' grief.""
- **Abstract says:** "if replicated, the findings indicate that CJS involvement may not significantly affect the mental health of bereaved people, raising questions about the generalizability of the framework of therapeutic jurisprudence…"
- **Problem:** The authors explicitly condition their conclusion on replication and frame it as raising questions; the pitch declares a cultural idea disproved on the basis of one observational cohort from a uniquely supported mass-casualty case. The digest's Caveats acknowledge replication is needed, so the pitch contradicts its own caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Pitch angle:** "Did the trial help? For MH17 families, the data say it made no measurable difference either way.""

---

### Study 11: How much you'd be blamed for *not* doing something predicts your behavior better than how much you'd be praised for doing it
**PMID:** 42655904 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

The body text is accurate: six studies, virtue/duty evaluations not systematically related, improved prediction of intended blood donation and actual voting, and the masking and paid-donation puzzles.

**Issue A. Headline states a comparison the study did not report** — Severity: Major

- **As written:** "How much you'd be blamed for *not* doing something predicts your behavior better than how much you'd be praised for doing it"
- **Abstract says:** "we show that a bivalent measure of moral evaluations (assessing the blame or praise for both doing and not doing the same act) allows for more accurate predictions of moral behaviors"
- **Problem:** The finding is that measuring *both* poles improves prediction — not that the blame-for-omission pole outperforms the praise-for-commission pole. The headline asserts a horse race the abstract never reports, and it contradicts the digest's own body text ("Measuring both improved predictions"). A pitch built on this hook would collapse on contact with the paper.
- **Suggested fix:** "Asking how much you'd be blamed for *not* doing something — as well as praised for doing it — predicts behaviour better than either question alone"

---

### Study 12: Brain waves recorded a week after a stroke predict who will still be recovering thinking skills six months later
**PMID:** 42663449 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=96, EEG at 8±1 days, MoCA at 3 and 6 months, 55.2% recovery, the counterintuitive direction of the frontal PAF and DTABR predictors, elevated DFV, AUC 0.831, the ≥2-point MoCA threshold and the stepwise-regression overfitting risk are all correctly reported and caveated.

**Issue A. Several supporting details cannot be checked against the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "rehabilitation is often withdrawn early on the basis of a poor three-month assessment" / "Tran Cong Thang and Nguyen Van Tuan at Ho Chi Minh City are the calls" / "single center"
- **Abstract says:** Reports only that early qEEG "could help inform personalized rehabilitation planning"; author list gives "Nguyen VT" and "Tran TC" with initials only; no statement that the cohort was single-site.
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. The clinical-practice premise (rehab withdrawal at three months) is the hinge of the "why it matters" and needs an independent source; the expanded Vietnamese author names are guesses from initials and are easy to get wrong in print; single-centre status is assumed.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rehabilitation decisions often hinge on a three-month assessment [source needed] … Contact the corresponding authors (Nguyen V.T., Cho Ray Hospital / Tran T.C., University of Medicine and Pharmacy at Ho Chi Minh City) — confirm full names before use."

---

### Study 13: Men and women's prolonged grief hangs together differently — identity loss is more central for men
**PMID:** 42635333 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=1,093 (274 men, mean age 37.03), PG-13-R, higher severity in women, similar global strength, significantly different network structure, and meaninglessness/disengagement as most central in both networks are all accurate.

**Issue A. "Significantly" attached to an untested comparison** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** ""identity disruption" — not knowing who you are without the person — was significantly more central in men"
- **Abstract says:** "Identity Disruption showed higher EI in males." (Significance values are reported only for network structure, M = 0.35, p = .018, and global strength, S = 0.75, p = .114.)
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a significance test for the overall network structure comparison, not for the identity-disruption centrality difference specifically. Calling that difference "significant" adds statistical weight the abstract does not supply.
- **Suggested fix:** ""identity disruption" — not knowing who you are without the person — was more central in men"

**Issue B. "Rather than on longing" is not in the data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "men's grief may hinge disproportionately on a loss of self rather than on longing"
- **Abstract says:** Reports centrality only for Meaninglessness, Disengagement and Identity Disruption; yearning/longing centrality is not mentioned.
- **Problem:** The contrast with longing is an editorial addition; nothing in the abstract compares identity disruption with yearning.
- **Suggested fix:** "men's grief may hinge disproportionately on a loss of self"

---

### Study 14: The brain's waste-clearance system looks more impaired in people on two antipsychotics than one
**PMID:** 42551238 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Group sizes (37 / 30 / 36), both patient groups below controls, the combination group lower still including the left hemisphere, and the DTI-ALPS proxy caveat are all correct. The "do not imply anyone should change medication" note is appropriate.

**Issue A. Direction of the cognitive correlation reversed relative to the abstract's wording** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Lower ALPS values correlated with worse cognitive performance."
- **Abstract says:** "Correlation analyses revealed that the bilateral mean ALPS index and the left hemisphere ALPS index were negatively correlated with cognitive function."
- **Problem:** As literally written, a *negative* correlation between ALPS and cognitive function means higher ALPS went with poorer cognitive function — the opposite of the digest's claim. The direction only matches the digest if the cognitive measure is scored so that higher = worse (a deficit or symptom scale), which the abstract does not specify. Either way, the digest cannot assert this direction from the abstract, and it is the link on which the whole "clogged drainage harms cognition" hook rests.
- **Suggested fix:** "ALPS values also correlated with cognitive test scores, though the abstract does not name the cognitive instrument or make the direction unambiguous — confirm with the authors before pitching."

---

### Study 15: Antipsychotic polypharmacy is rising again, 21 years of prescribing records show
**PMID:** 42551239 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Territory-wide EHR coverage 2004–2024, stable overall use, the FGA-to-SGA crossover, olanzapine at 20.6%, clozapine at 7.5%, and the polypharmacy trajectory (24.0% → 22.4% in 2011 → 28.0% in 2024) all match. The erratum and the industry disclosures (Amgen, GSK to ICKW; consulting fees) are appropriately carried into Caveats.

---

### Study 16: Insecure attachment predicts avoiding conversations about sexual consent
**PMID:** 42661106 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The model name, the two hypothesised mechanisms (mentalizing, emotion regulation/perceived costs), N=395, the mixed pathway support, and the authors' own call for testing alternate pathways are accurately represented, and the pitch explicitly frames it as preliminary theory-testing.

---

### Study 17: Autistic adults say talking to non-autistic people costs more effort — and noise makes them lose words
**PMID:** 42547992 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

NCATS instrument, 154 analysed responses from autistic adults aged 18–35, environmental effects, word loss/scripting/withdrawal, the greater effort and masking with allistic partners, and the Double Empathy Problem link are accurate. (The abstract notes 165 were surveyed and 154 responses analysed; the digest's figure is the analysed sample, which is fine.)

**Issue A. Authors' hedges dropped** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Most said environmental factors — crowding, noise, unfamiliarity — affected their communication" / "Negative emotions worsened communication regardless of who they were speaking to."
- **Abstract says:** "The majority of the participants noted that environmental factors, such as crowdedness, noise levels, and familiarity, at least somewhat impacted their communication" / "negative emotions such as stress, frustration, and anxiety may worsen communication difficulties regardless of the conversation partner's neurotype."
- **Problem:** "At least somewhat impacted" and "may worsen" are deliberately weak claims from self-reported reflective reports; the digest presents both as firm effects.
- **Suggested fix:** "Most said environmental factors — crowding, noise, unfamiliarity — at least somewhat affected their communication… Participants reported that negative emotions may worsen communication regardless of who they were speaking to."

**Issue B. Wider angle extrapolates to workplaces the study never sampled** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "open-plan environments were built on a theory of collaboration that appears to disable a substantial minority of workers."
- **Abstract says:** A reflective-report survey of 154 autistic adults about "past contextual conversations"; no workplace observation, no non-autistic comparison group, no measure of work performance.
- **Problem:** "Appears to disable a substantial minority of workers" presents a workplace conclusion the data cannot support — the study asked individuals to reflect on conversations, not on job function.
- **Suggested fix:** "open-plan environments were built on a theory of collaboration that autistic adults' own accounts suggest may make conversation harder for them."

### Study 18: Mental fatigue and physical fatigue push you off the sofa in completely different ways
**PMID:** 42543096 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Study 1 (n=675, Italian PES validation) and Study 2 (n=424, mean age 25.2, three-month longitudinal mediation) are accurately described, as is the dissociation: physical fatigue acting through approach/avoidance tendencies and strongest for vigorous activity, mental fatigue unrelated to those tendencies.

**Issue A. Direction of the mental-fatigue effect is asserted, not reported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Mental fatigue had no relationship with those approach/avoidance tendencies at all, but directly predicted less light and moderate activity."
- **Abstract says:** "mental fatigue was not associated with these tendencies but directly predicted light and moderate physical activity."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not state the sign of the direct effect. "Less" is the intuitive reading, but it is an assumption, and the whole "knowledge work erodes your walking" wider angle depends on it. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Mental fatigue had no relationship with those approach/avoidance tendencies at all, but directly predicted light and moderate activity — confirm the sign of that effect with the authors before pitching."
